title: Comments in marketStats.ts and types.ts contradict the bit-127-mask decoder in dataLayer.ts
description: Iter-4 fixed the ask-flag mask in dataLayer.ts:220-223 (good — verified empirically per synthesis-notes). But two of the three files involved still describe a different design. marketStats.ts:53-54 says 'For bids, the order_id decode is tautologically correct against test fixtures but wrong against real chain order_ids. Prefer injected price.' — implying the injection comes from somewhere other than the order_id. types.ts:72 doubles down: '/** Injected from companion OrderInfo/OrderPlaced event. Preferred over order_id decode. */'. Neither matches reality: the iter-4 injection is `Number((BigInt(orderIdStr) & ((1n<<127n)-1n)) >> 64n)` — it is itself an order_id decode, just a different formula than `decodeBidPrice`/`decodeAskPrice`. The dataLayer.ts:204-218 comment now correctly describes the bit-127-aware decode and even contradicts the chain-shape note ('the chain-shape prose's "inverted for bids" claim is contradicted by the captured data'). So three different stories about price decoding are now resident in three files.
impact: A future maintainer who sees a price discrepancy will read types.ts:72 and marketStats.ts:53, look for OrderInfo→Order plumbing in the data layer, find none, and either rewrite the wrong layer or add a redundant join. The doc/code drift recreates the original confusion the iter-2 review surfaced — and now it's worse, because there are three formulae claiming to be 'the' price decode (decodeAskPrice, decodeBidPrice, and the bit-127-mask in dataLayer), and the three docs disagree about which is canonical.
recommendation: Pick one story and apply it everywhere. Recommendation: (a) update types.ts:72 to '/** Decoded by the data layer from order_id high 64 bits with bit-127 ask-flag masked. Preferred over compute-time fallbacks. */'; (b) update marketStats.ts:53-54 to match: 'For bids, the order_id decode below uses the legacy chain-shape inversion formula; the data layer now decodes the same bits with the bit-127-mask formula and injects the result via Order.price.'; (c) consider whether decodeBidPrice and decodeAskPrice can be retired (they are only correct against the test fixtures' builder roundtrip — the data layer injection is canonical for chain inputs). Or, if both formulas must coexist, document precisely which inputs each is correct for.

title: App.tsx polling effect still calls setState after await without cancellation flag
description: Iter-3 R2-006 / R2-004 carried this forward; iter-4 did not address it. The initial-load effect (lines 41-87) now correctly uses `let cancelled = false` and checks it before each setState (lines 76, 80). The polling effect (lines 91-125) does NOT — its `async` setInterval callback awaits Promise.allSettled (line 98), then unconditionally calls `setState({...})` at line 121. The cleanup callback at line 124 only runs `clearInterval`; it does not flip a cancellation flag, so an in-flight tick that fires immediately before unmount can call setState on an unmounted component. This is the exact stale-state-update hazard called out in iter-2 R2-007 and iter-3 R2-004; iter-4's main-tsx refactor leaves it untouched.
impact: React 19 logs a warning rather than erroring, but the latent bug is real: under HMR, in tests that mount/unmount the component, or any reload-driven remount, a polling tick from the previous mount can stomp on the new mount's state. The two effects also still re-implement the same ~30 lines of pipeline (sentinel-card construction at lines 54-68 vs 102-115; poolErrors collection at lines 72-74 vs 117-119) — any future change to one diverges silently from the other.
recommendation: Add `let cancelled = false; return () => { cancelled = true; clearInterval(intervalId); };` to the polling effect, and gate the setState at line 121 on `if (!cancelled)`. Better, factor the shared pipeline into a private helper: `function refreshAll(deps, pools): Promise<{ cards, poolErrors }>` and have both effects call it. This eliminates ~30 LOC of duplication AND makes the cancellation discipline a single point.

title: resolvePoolInnerFields still conflates four shape variants under one signature
description: Iter-2 R2-004 (medium), iter-3 R2-003 (medium), and now iter-4: resolvePoolInnerFields returns four structurally different sub-shapes under one Promise<Record<string, unknown> | null> signature. Branch 1 (line 117) is the production code-path branching on whether the response shape happens to match the T-014 unit-test fixture (`if 'book' in fields`). Branch 2-3 fall through `inner` then `versionedFields` traversal with implicit fallbacks (`return fields // degraded`). Branch 4 returns `wrapperFields` if the dynamic-field PoolInner shape lacks a `book` key (line 152). buildPoolInnerState at line 268 still has to defensively `(field?.fields ?? field)` everywhere because the caller cannot tell which variant resolvePoolInnerFields returned. Iter-4 did not touch this function.
impact: Same as iter-3: any future change to one of the four shapes silently switches branches. The fixture-aware branch (`if 'book' in fields return fields`) means a real chain response that accidentally has a top-level `book` field would skip the dynamic-field traversal entirely and the code path would degrade silently with no log.
recommendation: Same as iter-2/iter-3: split into two functions with crisp contracts — `resolvePoolInnerFromVersioned(rpcUrl, poolId): Promise<PoolInnerFields>` (production; throws if traversal fails) and `resolvePoolInnerFromDirect(obj): PoolInnerFields | null` (fixture path). Have buildPoolInnerState branch explicitly. Or change the T-014 fixture to return the realistic Pool wrapper shape so the production code path has one variant.

title: dataLayer.ts still imports PoolCardData from a UI component file
description: Iter-2 R2-002, iter-3 R2-005, iter-4: dataLayer.ts imports PoolCardData from `./components/PoolCard.js`, inverting the natural dependency direction (data layer depending on UI components). main.tsx no longer needs PoolCardData (it imports PoolDescriptor from manifest and lets the deps flow through), but dataLayer.ts:21 still has the inverted import. types.ts:14 still claims to be the home of `UI aggregate types (PoolCardData)` but PoolCardData is still declared in components/PoolCard.tsx:16-25. Iter-4 did not touch this; the half-applied single-source-of-truth fix from H-10 persists.
impact: Same as iter-3: structurally same shape as a circular dependency, broken only by file-load ordering accident. If anyone moves PoolCard or splits it into sub-components, the data layer breaks. The types.ts header comment is a documented lie until PoolCardData actually moves there.
recommendation: Move PoolCardData and SparklinePoint declarations to types.ts (which already documents itself as their home) and have PoolCard.tsx import them as `import type { PoolCardData, SparklinePoint } from '../types.js'`. Then dataLayer.ts imports PoolCardData from types.ts and the dependency direction matches the conceptual layering.

title: FillRecord/RawFillEvent twin types and no-op map survive iter-4
description: FillRecord (fillAggregator.ts:9-14) and RawFillEvent (fillFetcher.ts:19-24) are structurally identical (poolId, timestampMs, baseQuantity, price), declared in two modules, forcing the no-op map at dataLayer.ts:397-402. Iter-4 did not touch any of the three. The drift hazard remains: any new field added to one type but not the other is silently lost in the map. types.ts:14 still mentions `RawFillEntry` (which exists in types.ts:94) but neither RawFillEvent nor FillRecord lives in types.ts.
impact: Three places to update if a fifth field is ever needed. The map function is dead weight that would silently swallow any future field divergence. Reader friction for anyone tracing the fill data flow across the fetcher → dataLayer → aggregator boundary.
recommendation: Move one canonical FillRecord (or RawFillEvent — pick one name) into types.ts. fillFetcher and fillAggregator both import it. Drop the no-op `.map(f => ({...}))` in dataLayer.ts:397-402 and pass rawFills directly to aggregateFills.

title: manifest.ts still re-exports types from types.ts; two canonical paths persist
description: Iter-2 R2-010, iter-3 R2-009, iter-4: manifest.ts re-exports PoolDescriptor and LoadedManifest from types.ts (line 22) while also importing them (line 23). Both App.tsx (line 14) and dataLayer.ts (line 19) import these types from manifest.ts; main.tsx (line 22) imports PoolDescriptor from manifest.ts as well. Verified by grep: three import sites all use './manifest.js' as the canonical path for these types, not './types.js'. The single-source-of-truth promise of types.ts is undermined.
impact: Consolidator (and human reader) cannot tell which file is canonical for these types just by reading imports. Doubles the surface area for type drift. If a future change adds a field to PoolDescriptor in types.ts but a stale local copy is later re-introduced in manifest.ts, the discrepancy will only surface as a structural type mismatch.
recommendation: Drop the re-export from manifest.ts:22, update App.tsx (line 14), main.tsx (line 22), and dataLayer.ts (line 19) to import directly from './types.js'. Three-line change.
evidence:
export type { PoolDescriptor, LoadedManifest } from './types.js';
import type { LoadedManifest, PoolDescriptor } from './types.js';

title: console.warn in dataLayer.ts couples pure data layer to global console
description: Iter-4 addressed iter-3 R2-011 (silent BigInt try/catch) by adding `console.warn` in two paths (non-finite Number coercion at line 231; BigInt SyntaxError at line 240). This solves the silent-failure concern, but it does so by coupling a previously-pure data layer to the global `console` object. There is no injectable logger; tests cannot observe or silence these warnings without intercepting `globalThis.console.warn`. The rest of dataLayer.ts uses thrown Errors with descriptive messages (rpc(), resolvePoolInnerFields()) — adding console.warn here is the first non-throw observability primitive in the module, with no consistency with the surrounding error idiom.
impact: Test output (vitest) will have warnings printed when fixture-shaped order_ids exceed Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER if any future test exercises that path. CI logs become noisier without a way to selectively silence. More importantly: any caller wanting structured observability (e.g. an error counter, a Sentry breadcrumb, a 'degraded mode' indicator in the UI) cannot see these warnings — they go to the void of console output. The injectable-logger pattern is a known fix; bolting console.warn onto an otherwise-DI'd layer is an inconsistency.
recommendation: Either (a) add an optional `logger?: { warn: (msg: string) => void }` to RunDataLayerArgs and pass it through to traverseBigVector, defaulting to console; or (b) accept the inconsistency but extract a tiny `logDecodeFailure(orderIdStr, reason)` helper at module scope so the warning shape is consistent and a single point of edit can later route to a real logger. Option (a) is the disciplined choice; option (b) is the minimal change.

title: main.tsx buildDeps factory still encodes ordering invariant only at runtime
description: Iter-4 fixed the iter-3 R2-002 'closure-over-let with module-level cachedPackageId' smell — the new buildDeps() factory captures `let packageId: string | undefined` in the closure and exposes loadManifest + fetchPoolStats sharing it. This is a genuine improvement; no module-level mutable. However, the wiring still encodes the ordering invariant 'loadManifest must resolve before fetchPoolStats is called' at runtime (line 55 throws if `packageId === undefined`). The type system does not encode this — a caller can still call fetchPoolStats first and get a thrown Error rather than a compile-time refusal. The throw is observable (better than the iter-3 silent empty-string packageId), but it's a runtime check for what could be a structural one.
impact: Friendly degradation: fetchPoolStats called before loadManifest now throws a clear actionable error instead of silently fetching against an empty packageId. The remaining concern is structural: the type AppDeps doesn't tell App.tsx that one method is a precondition for the other. App.tsx happens to await loadManifest first (line 46) before any fetchPoolStats call (line 51), so the invariant holds — but it's enforced by App.tsx's discipline, not by the type system.
recommendation: If the type-level fix matters: change the deps shape to a one-step `init(): Promise<{ pools: PoolDescriptor[]; fetchPoolStats: (d: PoolDescriptor) => Promise<PoolCardData> }>` so the contract bakes in the ordering. Lower-cost: leave as-is; the runtime throw is descriptive and the invariant is exercised by the App's actual usage. Treat this as info-level; the iter-3 finding is genuinely closed.

title: vite.config.ts manifest path still hard-coded to home-relative layout
description: Iter-2 R2-008, iter-3 R2-007, iter-4: the manifest disk path is hard-coded as `~/workspace/deepbook-sandbox/sandbox/deployments/localnet.json`, coupling the dev server to a specific workspace layout that the contract section 'Integration / sandbox contract' said should be configurable per-environment. Iter-4 did not touch vite.config.ts.
impact: Friction for any developer whose checkout is not at exactly that path. Mitigated by the 404 response surfacing the expected path in the error JSON (line 40), so failure is at least debuggable.
recommendation: Read from an env var with the current default. `const MANIFEST_DISK_PATH = process.env.SANDBOX_MANIFEST_PATH ?? path.join(homedir(), 'workspace', 'deepbook-sandbox', 'sandbox', 'deployments', 'localnet.json');`. Document `SANDBOX_MANIFEST_PATH` in the README/runbook.

title: rpcId module-level mutable counter persists across iter-4
description: Iter-1 R2-010, iter-2 R2-009, iter-3 R2-008, iter-4: `let rpcId = 0;` at module scope. Inert today (JSON-RPC ids only need uniqueness within a connection), but global mutable state in a module that otherwise consciously injects state via args. Iter-4 did not touch it.
impact: Negligible at runtime. Slightly harder to reason about than necessary; would silently couple any future test that asserts on the id to test-execution order.
recommendation: Move into a closure created per `runDataLayer` invocation, or use `crypto.randomUUID()` / `Date.now()` for the id.

title: fetchSinglePoolStats alias-as-fetchPoolStats still ships in iter-4
description: Iter-2 R2-011, iter-3 R2-010, iter-4: `async function fetchPoolStats` (line 372) plus `export { fetchPoolStats as fetchSinglePoolStats };` (line 461). main.tsx imports it as fetchSinglePoolStats; runDataLayer (line 442) calls it as fetchPoolStats. Iter-4 did not pick a single name.
impact: Reader friction for anyone tracing the function across module boundaries. Search-and-replace tooling will miss one of the two names.
recommendation: Pick one name. Drop the alias export. The export-as-rename is one line; renaming the internal function is the more honest change.

title: Iter-4 confirms bit-127 ask-flag mask is now correctly wired
description: Confirmation finding for iter-4. The iter-3 R2-005 / R1-001 critical (bit-127 ask flag missing from injected price) is structurally addressed in iter-4 by `Number((BigInt(orderIdStr) & ASK_FLAG_MASK) >> 64n)` where `ASK_FLAG_MASK = (1n << 127n) - 1n`. This decodes both bid and ask order_ids correctly per the synthesis-notes empirical verification (bid 12377783720203182843884075 → 671000; ask 170141183460486719245069180370816077150 → 948000). The iter-3 silent-fallback hazard (R2-011) is also addressed by the new console.warn calls, though see R2-007 for the design concern about the logger-injection pattern. The deps-mutation closure smell (iter-3 R2-002) is closed by the buildDeps() factory, see R2-008 for the residual concern. Net: the three highest-priority iter-3 findings are structurally resolved; the design carry-forwards (R2-001, R2-002, R2-003 in this report) are the work that remains.
impact: Iter-3 R2-002 (deps mutation) and iter-3 R2-005/R1-001 (bit-127 mask) and iter-3 R2-011 (silent BigInt) should be considered closed. Remaining concerns are doc/code drift (R2-001 in this report), the polling-effect cancellation (R2-002 in this report), and the layered-types cleanups (R2-003..R2-006 in this report).
recommendation: No action on these specific fixes. Address the new and carried-forward findings above as separate work.
